Main.sentence: The Federal Insurance Contributions Act ( FICA /ˈfaɪkə/ ) is a ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ federal ___E:payroll U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payroll_tax)___ (or employment) tax payable by both employees and employers to fund ___E:Social Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States))___ and ___E:Medicare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States))___  —federal programs that provide benefits for retirees, people with disabilities, and children of deceased workers.

The Federal Insurance Contributions Act is a tax mechanism ___E:codified U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codification_(law))___ in ___E:Title 26 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Code)___ , Subtitle C, Chapter 21 of the ___E:United States Code U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Code)___ .

Social security benefits include old-age, survivors, and ___E:disability insurance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_insurance)___ (OASDI); Medicare provides hospital insurance benefits for the elderly.
The amount that one pays in payroll taxes throughout one's working career is associated indirectly with the social security benefits annuity that one receives as a retiree.

Consequently, ___E:Kevin Hassett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Hassett)___ wrote that FICA is not a tax because its collection is directly tied to benefits that one is entitled to collect later in life.  However, the ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ ruled in Flemming v. Nestor (1960) that the Social Security system is neither a pension nor an insurance program and that no one has an accrued property right to benefits from the system regardless of how much that person may have contributed.
FICA therefore behaves as a tax for all practical purposes, earmarked for particular uses by Congress but fully subject to Congressional authority, including redirection.
The FICA tax applies to earned income only and is not imposed on investment income such as rental income, interest, or dividends.

The Hospital Insurance (HI) portion of FICA, which funds ___E:Medicare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States))___ Part A hospital benefits, applies to all earned income, while the OASDI portion of the tax is imposed on earned income only up to cap annually set by Congress ($160,200 in 2023).

In 2004, the ___E:Center on Budget and Policy Priorities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_on_Budget_and_Policy_Priorities)___ stated that three-quarters of taxpayers pay more in payroll taxes than they do in income taxes.

FICA is subject to neither the ___E:standard deduction U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_deduction)___ nor any personal exemption and so is generally considered to be a ___E:regressive tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regressive_tax)___ .

Since 1990, the employee's share of the Social Security portion of the FICA tax has been 6.2% of gross compensation up to a limit that adjusts with inflation. [a]  The taxation limit in 2020 was $137,700 of gross compensation, resulting in a maximum Social Security tax for 2020 of $8,537.40.  This limit, known as the ___E:Social Security Wage Base U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_Wage_Base)___ , goes up each year based on average national wages and, in general, at a faster rate than the ___E:Consumer Price Index U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_Price_Index)___ (CPI-U).

The employee's share of the Medicare portion of the tax is 1.45% of wages, with no limit on the amount of wages subject to the Medicare portion of the tax.  Because some payroll compensation may be subject to federal and state income tax withholding in addition to Social Security tax withholding and Medicare tax withholding, the Social Security and Medicare taxes often account for only a portion of the total an employee pays.

The employer is also liable for 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare taxes,  making the total Social Security tax 12.4% of wages and the total Medicare tax 2.9%. (Self-employed people are responsible for the entire FICA percentage of 15.3% (= 12.4% + 2.9%), since they are in a sense both the employer and the employed; see the section on ___E:self-employed people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Self-employed_people)___ for more details.)

If a worker starts a new ___E:job U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Employment)___ halfway through the year and during that year has already earned an amount exceeding the Social Security tax wage base limit with the old employer, the new employer is not allowed to stop ___E:withholding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withholding)___ until the wage base limit has been earned with the new employer (that is, without regard to the wage base limit earned under the old employer).
There are some limited cases, such as a successor-predecessor employer transfer, in which the payments that have already been withheld can be counted toward the year-to-date total.

If a worker has overpaid toward Social Security by having more than one job or by having switched jobs during the year, that worker can file a request to have that overpayment counted as a credit for tax paid when he or she files a ___E:federal income tax return U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_tax_in_the_United_States)___ .
If the taxpayer is due a ___E:refund U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_refund)___ , then the FICA tax overpayment is refunded.

A tax similar to the FICA tax is imposed on the earnings of ___E:self-employed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-employment)___ individuals, such as ___E:independent contractors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_contractor)___ and members of a ___E:partnership U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership)___ .

This tax is imposed not by the Federal Insurance Contributions Act but instead by the Self-Employment Contributions Act of 1954 (SECA), which is codified as Chapter 2 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code, ___E:26 U.S.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Code)___ ___E:§ 1401 U:(https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1401)___ through ___E:26 U.S.C. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Code)___ ___E:§ 1403 U:(https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1403)___ (the "SE Tax Act").

Under the SE Tax Act, self-employed people are responsible for the entire percentage of 15.3% (= 12.4% [Soc. Sec.] + 2.9% [Medicare]); however, the 15.3% multiplier is applied to 92.35% of the business's net earnings from self-employment , rather than 100% of the gross earnings; the difference, 7.65%, is half of the 15.3%, and makes the calculation fair in comparison to that of regular (non-self-employed) employees.

SECA requires self-employed individuals in the United States to pay ___E:Social Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States))___ and ___E:Medicare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States))___ taxes.
If a self-employed individual has net earnings of $400 or more in a tax year, they are generally required to pay SECA taxes.
Self-employed individuals are responsible for paying both the employer and employee portions of these taxes.
However, exceptions and specific rules may apply based on the nature of self-employment and individual circumstances.

Some student workers are exempt from FICA tax.  Students enrolled at least half-time in a university and working part-time for the same university are exempted from FICA payroll taxes if and only if their relationship with the university is primarily an educational one.  In order to be exempt from FICA payroll taxes, a student's work must be "incident to" the pursuit of a course of study, which is rarely the case with full-time employment.
However full-time college students are never exempt from FICA taxes on work performed off-campus.

___E:Medical residents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_resident)___ working full-time are not considered students and are not exempt from FICA payroll taxes, according to a ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ ruling in 2011.

A student enrolled and regularly attending classes at a school, college, or university who performs work as a cook, waiter, butler, maid, janitor, laundress, furnaceman, handyman, gardener, housekeeper, housemother, or similar duties in or around the club rooms or house of a local college club, or in or about the club rooms or house of a local chapter of a college fraternity or sorority, are exempt from FICA tax.  If the location's primary purpose is to provide room or board, however, then the work is subject to FICA tax.  Performing these services for an alumni club or alumni chapter also does not qualify for the exemption from FICA tax.

A number of state and local employers and their employees in the states of Alaska, California, Colorado, Illinois, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas are currently exempt from paying the Social Security portion of FICA taxes.
They provide alternative retirement and pension plans to their employees.
FICA initially did not apply to state and local governments, which were later given the option of participating.
Over time, most have elected to participate, but a substantial number remain outside the system.

Payments to members of a ___E:federally recognized Native American tribe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_federally_recognized_tribes)___ for services performed as council members are not subject to FICA.

If a member of a federally recognized Native American tribe that has recognized fishing rights or a qualified Native American entity employs another member of the same Native American tribe for a fishing rights-related activity, the wages are exempt from FICA.
Some ___E:nonresident aliens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien_(law)#United_States)___ are exempt from FICA tax.

Members of certain religious groups, such as the ___E:Mennonites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites)___ and the ___E:Amish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amish)___ , may apply to be exempt from paying FICA tax.   These religious groups consider ___E:insurance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance)___ to be a lack of trust in God, and see it as their religious duty to provide for members who are sick, disabled, or elderly.
In order to apply to become exempt from paying FICA tax under this provision, the person must file Form 4029, which certifies that the person:

People who claim the above exemption must agree to notify the Internal Revenue Service within 60 days of either leaving the religious group or no longer following the established teachings of the religious group.

When a person temporarily works outside their country of origin, the person may be covered under two different countries' social security programs for the same work.  In order to relieve a person of double-taxation, the certain countries and the United States have entered into tax treaties, known as ___E:totalization agreements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalization_agreements)___ .

Aliens whose employer sends them to the United States on a temporary work assignment may be exempt from paying FICA tax on their earnings from working in the United States if there is a totalization agreement between the United States and the worker's home country.

Countries who have such a tax treaty with the United States include ___E:Australia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia)___ ,  ___E:Austria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria)___ ,  ___E:Belgium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium)___ ,  ___E:Canada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)___ ,  ___E:Chile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile)___ ,  ___E:Czech Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic)___ ,  ___E:Denmark U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark)___ ,  ___E:Finland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland)___ ,  ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ ,  ___E:Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany)___ ,  ___E:Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece)___ ,  ___E:Hungary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary)___ ,  ___E:Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland)___ ,  ___E:Japan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan)___ ,  ___E:Luxembourg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg)___ ,  ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ ,  ___E:Norway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway)___ ,  ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland)___ ,  ___E:Portugal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal)___ ,  ___E:Slovakia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia)___ ,  ___E:South Korea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea)___ ,  ___E:Spain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain)___ ,  ___E:Sweden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden)___ ,  ___E:Switzerland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland)___ ,  and ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ .

In order to claim an exemption from paying FICA tax, the alien worker must be on a temporary assignment of no more than five years and the alien worker must have a certificate from the country stating that the worker will continue to be covered by the country's social security system while the worker is in the United States.

When a parent employs a child under age 18 (or under age 21 for ___E:domestic service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_service)___ ), payments to the child are exempt from FICA tax.   The exemption also applies when a child is employed by a ___E:partnership U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership)___ in which each partner is a parent of the child.
The exemption does not apply when the child is employed by a ___E:corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation)___ or a partnership with partners who are not the child's parent.

Foreign governments are exempt from FICA tax on payments to their employees.  ___E:International organizations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization)___ are also exempt if the organization is listed in the ___E:International Organizations Immunities Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organizations_Immunities_Act)___ .
If an employee is a U.S. citizen, then the employee must typically pay self-employment tax on earnings from work performed in the United States.

If a state or local government pays individuals for services performed to be relieved from unemployment, the payments to the individuals are exempt from FICA tax.  The services must not be performed by individuals under other types of programs.
Payments are not exempt from FICA tax if the program's primary purpose is to increase an individual's chances of employment by providing training and work experience.

Payments to inmates of a prison for services performed for the state or local government that operates the prison are exempt from FICA tax, regardless of the location where the services are performed.

Services performed as part of a work-release program are exempt from FICA tax if and only if the individuals are not considered employees under common law, such as when the individual has control over what work is done and how the work it is done.

Payments to patients of an institution for services performed for the state of local government that operates the institution are exempt from FICA tax.   Services performed by patients as part of an institution's rehabilitative program or therapeutic program are exempt from FICA tax.

If a state or local government's employees were hired on a temporary basis in response to a specific unforeseen fire, storm, snow, earthquake, flood, or a similar emergency, and the employee is not intended to become a permanent employee, then payments to that employee are exempt from FICA tax.   In order to qualify for the exemption from FICA tax, the employee must have been hired to work temporarily in connection with an unforeseen emergency, such as an individual temporarily hired to battle a major forest fire, to respond to a volcano eruption, or to help people affected by a severe earthquake or flood.
Regular long-term police employees and regular long-term fire employees do not qualify under this particular exemption from FICA tax.
Payments to ___E:newspaper carriers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper_carrier)___ under age 18 are exempt from FICA tax.

Compensation for ___E:real estate agents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate_agent)___ and ___E:salespeople U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salesperson)___ is exempt from FICA tax under certain circumstances.

The compensation is exempt if substantially all compensation is directly related to sales or other output, rather than to the number of hours worked, and there is a written contract stating that the individuals will not be treated as employees for federal tax purposes.
The individual must typically pay self-employment tax on the compensation.
Prior to the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ , the following presented difficulties for Americans:

In the 1930s, the ___E:New Deal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal)___ introduced ___E:Social Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States))___ to rectify the first three problems (retirement, injury-induced disability, or congenital disability).
It introduced the FICA tax as the means to pay for Social Security.
In the 1960s, ___E:Medicare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States))___ was introduced to rectify the fourth problem (health care for the elderly).
The FICA tax was increased in order to pay for this expense.

In December 2010, as part of the legislation that extended the Bush tax cuts (called the ___E:Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Relief,_Unemployment_Insurance_Reauthorization,_and_Job_Creation_Act_of_2010)___ ), the government negotiated a temporary, one-year reduction in the FICA payroll tax. In February 2012, the tax cut was extended for another year.
Under FICA, the payroll tax applies to "wages" (defined by the act as "remuneration for employment").
In 2014, the Supreme Court unanimously held in United States v. Quality Stores, Inc. that severance pay is taxable wages for FICA purposes.

In August ___E:2020 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_in_United_States_politics_and_government)___ , President Donald Trump signed an executive order to temporarily suspend collection of the tax from September to December 2020. Critics feared this would lead to more underfunding of the ___E:Social Security Trust Fund U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_Trust_Fund)___ and Medicare trust fund.
The Social Security component of the FICA tax is ___E:regressive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regressive_tax)___ .
That is, the effective tax rate regresses, or decreases, as income increases beyond the compensation limit or wage base limit amount.

The Social Security component is a ___E:flat tax U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_tax)___ for wage levels under the Social Security Wage Base (see ___E:"Regular" employees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#"Regular"_employees_(most_wage-earners))___ above).
Because no tax is owed on wages above the wage base limit amount, the total tax rate declines as wages increase beyond that limit.
In other words, for wage levels above the limit, the absolute dollar amount of tax owed remains constant.

The earnings above the wage base limit amount are not, however, taken into account in the Primary Insurance Amount (PIA) to determine benefits payable under the various insurance programs of social security.

The FICA tax also is not imposed on ___E:unearned income U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unearned_income)___ , including interest on savings deposits, stock dividends, and capital gains such as profits from the sale of stock or real estate.
The proportion of total income that is exempt from FICA tax as "unearned income" tends to rise with higher income brackets.

Some, including ___E:Third Way U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Way_(United_States))___ , argue that since Social Security taxes are eventually returned to taxpayers, with interest, in the form of Social Security benefits, the regressiveness of the tax is effectively negated.
That is, the taxpayer gets back (more or less) what they put into the Social Security system.

Others, including The Economist and the ___E:Congressional Budget Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_Office)___ , point out that the Social Security system as a whole is ___E:progressive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_tax)___ in the lower income brackets.

Individuals with lower lifetime average wages receive a larger benefit (as both a percentage of their lifetime average wage income and a percentage of Social Security taxes paid) than do individuals with higher lifetime average wages; but for some lower earners, shorter lifetimes may negate the benefits.
